'''King:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} | title = [[List of governors of New Mexico|Governor]] | before_election = [[Bruce King]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Gary Johnson]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNM}} The '''1994 New Mexico gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 1994, for the four-year term beginning on January 1, 1995. Candidates for governor and lieutenant governor ran on a [[Ticket (election)|ticket]] as [[running mate]]s. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Bruce King]] ran for a fourth term with [[Patricia Madrid]] as a running mate, losing to [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominees [[Gary Johnson]], a businessman, and [[Walter Dwight Bradley|Walter Bradley]], a former [[New Mexico Senate|state senator]]. Former Lieutenant Governor [[Roberto Mondragón]] ran with [[Steven Schmidt]] as the nominees of the Green Party, receiving 10.4 percent of the vote. The election was marked by the surprising rise of [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Gary Johnson]], the 41-year-old owner of one of the state's largest construction companies. Johnson, who had never before held elected office, upset a crowded Republican primary field by a margin of fewer than 1,300 votes. With the state's non-Republicans split between the centrist King and progressive Mondragón, King failed to gain a majority and Johnson won the election with 49.8% of the vote.{{Cite magazine|last=Birnbaum|first=Ben|date=2016-08-12|title=Gary Johnson Has a Plan|url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2016/08/gary-johnson-profile-2016-libertarian-third-party-214162/|magazine=[[Politico Magazine]]|language=en|issn=2381-1595}} This is the last time a governor of New Mexico lost re-election. This was one of four gubernatorial elections where an incumbent Democrat was defeated in 1994. ==Primary election== ===Democratic Party=== King faced a tough renomination campaign, being challenged by incumbent Lieutenant Governor Casey Luna, who had a falling out with King in 1993 over King's refusal to give Luna a larger role in King's administration.{{cite web |title=Luna Won't Take Sides in the Race |url=https://santafenewmexican.newspaperarchive.com/santa-fe-new-mexican/1994-10-25/page-2/ |website=Santa Fe New Mexican |date=25 October 1994|access-date=18 September 2019}} Former [[New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands]] [[Jim Baca]] also challenged King. ====Candidates==== * [[Jim Baca]], former Director of the U.S. [[Bureau of Land Management]] and former [[New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands]] * [[Bruce King]], incumbent Governor * [[Casey Luna]], incumbent Lieutenant Governor ====Results==== {{Election box begin no change| title = Democratic primary results{{Cite web|title=Canvass of Returns of Primary Election Held on June 7, 1994 – State of New Mexico |url=https://klvg4oyd4j.execute-api.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/prod/PublicFiles/ee3072ab0d43456cb15a51f7d82c77a2/50418c58-4d9b-4fd4-9f56-fad815f843dd/CanvassPrimary1994.pdf |publisher=New Mexico Secretary of State|access-date=July 29, 2024}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Bruce King]] (incumbent) | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 76,039 | percentage = 38.38% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Casey Luna]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 71,364 | percentage = 36.45% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Jim Baca]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 48,401 | percentage = 24.72% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 195,804 | percentage= 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} ===Republican Party=== ====Candidates==== * [[David F. Cargo]], former [[Governor of New Mexico|Governor]] (1967{{En dash}}71) and former [[New Mexico House of Representatives|State Representative]] * [[Richard Cheney (New Mexico politician)|Dick Cheney]], [[New Mexico House of Representatives|State Representative]] from [[Farmington, New Mexico|Farmington]] * [[John Dendahl]], former New Mexico Secretary of Economic Development and Tourism * [[Gary Johnson]], businessman ===== Declined ===== * [[Manuel Lujan Jr.]], former U.S. Representative from [[Albuquerque, New Mexico|Albuquerque]] (1969{{En dash}}89) and [[United States Secretary of the Interior|U.S. Secretary of the Interior]] (1989{{En dash}}93) ==== Campaign ==== Cheney ran on a platform highlighting cracking down on violent crime, repealing the gasoline tax, and lowering public spending.{{cite web |title=Albuquerque Journal from Albuquerque, New Mexico · Page 7 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/157736061/}} During the campaign, he controversially changed his legal name from Richard to "Dick". Opponents including [[John Dendahl]] stated that people voting in the polls would confuse Cheney with the former Secretary of Defense [[Dick Cheney]] from [[Wyoming]], improving his chances of winning the primary. Public polling after the change showed that his numbers increased significantly.{{cite web |title=The Santa Fe New Mexican from Santa Fe, New Mexico · Page 7 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/211714360/}} At the state convention, Cheney received 49% of the vote against 29% for Dendahl and 22% for Johnson.{{cite book |last=Morehouse |first=Sarah McCally |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1rd0Eqt7sUYC&q=cheney&pg=PA258 |title=The Governor as Party Leader: Campaigning and Governing |publisher=University of Michigan Press |year=1998 |isbn=0472108484 |via=Google Books}} ====Results==== {{Election box begin no change | title = June 7, 1994 Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Gary Johnson]] | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 32,091 | percentage = 34.48% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Richard Cheney (New Mexico politician)|Dick Cheney]] | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 30,811 | percentage = 33.10% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate =[[John Dendahl]] | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 18,007 | percentage = 19.35% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[David F. Cargo]] | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 12,105 | percentage = 13.01% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Keith Russell Judd]] (write-in) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 57 | percentage = 0.06% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 93,071 | percentage= 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} ==General election== ===Candidates=== * [[Gary Johnson]], businessman (Republican) * [[Bruce King]], incumbent Governor (Democratic) * [[Roberto Mondragón]], former [[Lieutenant Governor of New Mexico|Lieutenant Governor]] (Green) === Campaign === Bruce King, the Democratic three-term incumbent{{efn|Non-consecutive terms}}, began the general election with the most funding and name recognition.{{Cn|date=May 2021}} King was a career politician who had first been elected to the [[Santa Fe County, New Mexico#Government|Santa Fe County Commission]] in 1954, when Gary Johnson was just one year old.{{Cite news |last=Terrell |first=Steve |date=2020-01-14 |title=After big loss, experts doubt King will run for office again |url=http://www.santafenewmexican.com/news/local_news/after-big-loss-experts-doubt-king-will-run-for-office/article_d29cd7bf-c629-5359-895b-dfe2b4c06a6b.html |access-date=2021-05-10 |work=[[The Santa Fe New Mexican]] |quote=Bruce King began his political career in 1954 when he won a seat on the Santa Fe County Commission.}} King also had the support of the Gold Boot Club, a business-backed political coalition that channeled thousands of dollars to his campaign.{{Cite news |last=Kurtz |first=Josh |date=1994-10-26 |title=The Liberals' Dilemma: Choose Your Poison |url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/2941962/ |url-access=limited |work=[[The Santa Fe Reporter]] |page=33 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} King's quest for an unprecedented fourth term faced obstacles from the left and the right. From the left, King was challenged by [[Green Party (United States)|Green Party]] nominee Roberto Mondragón. Mondragón was a [[populism|populist]] former Democrat, who had served as [[Lieutenant Governor of New Mexico|Lieutenant Governor]] from 1971 to 1975 and in the state [[New Mexico House of Representatives|House]] from 1979 to 1983.{{Cn|date=May 2021}} Mondragón had a knack for appealing to both progressive whites and working-class Hispanics, and attacked King for his cushy relationships with big business. Gary Johnson was the nominee of New Mexico's Republican Party, a statewide party that had won just [[List of governors of New Mexico|one gubernatorial election]] since 1970. Johnson faced the challenge of keeping together his Republican base while appealing to independents and Democrats frustrated with King. Johnson campaigned as a political outsider and self-made entrepreneur.{{Cn|date=May 2021}} In college, Johnson had worked as a door-to-door handyman, a business that gradually expanded into Big J Enterprises. By 1999, the company employed over 1,000 people and was worth several million dollars.{{Cite news |last=Marciello |first=Alex |date=2011-02-25 |title=Former NM governor talks politics |url=http://www.newburyportnews.com/news/local_news/former-nm-governor-talks-politics/article_014bc109-0b14-56a0-a82e-96ca5737caf9.html |access-date=2021-05-10 |work=The Daily News of Newburyport |quote=Prior to that, he was the CEO and founder of Big J Enterprises, a business that grew out of his door-to-door work as a handyman during college. By the time he sold the company in 1999, it had more than 1,000 employees and was a multimillion-dollar enterprise.}} Johnson avoided then-divisive social issues like [[abortion]] and [[gay rights]], and focused his campaign on pocketbook issues like taxes and the state budget. Johnson touted his experience in the business world of balancing budgets while growing his company, and promised to bring that experience to state government.{{Cite news |last=Lyman |first=Andy |date=2016-04-20 |title=How Gary Johnson went from 'Governor No' to third party icon |url=http://nmpoliticalreport.com/40453/gary-johnson-profile/ |work=New Mexico Political Report}} In November, Gary Johnson won the election with just under 50% of the vote, while King got almost 40% and Mondragón pulled in just over 10%. === Polling === {| class="wikitable" |- valign= bottom ! style="width:210px;"| Poll source ! style="width:190px;"| Date(s)
